# Get Plain-English Explanations of Any Contract With Claude

> **In short:** You can paste a contract — rental agreement, terms of service, employment offer — into Claude and ask for a plain-language summary. It's free to try, takes about 10 minutes the first time, and Claude can't replace a lawyer, but it can save you an hour of squinting at dense legal text.

Got a 30-page PDF that nobody on Earth would actually read end-to-end? You can hand the text to Claude and ask, in your own words, "what does this actually say?" This guide walks through the whole flow: getting the contract text onto your screen, dropping it into Claude, and asking the right questions. No legal background needed.

## Before you start
- **A Claude account**, free or paid — sign up at `claude.ai`. The free plan covers most personal use. Paid plans have a larger context window, which helps with very long contracts.
- **The contract itself**, ideally a digital copy (PDF, email attachment, or webpage). Photos of paper pages are much harder for Claude to work with because the text has to be read off the image.
- **A way to extract the text** if it's a PDF. Most computers let you select and copy text from a PDF directly. If yours doesn't, a free online "PDF to text" tool works.
- **Rough total time**: 10–15 minutes the first time, around 5 minutes once you've done it once.

> ⚠️ **What Claude can't do.** Claude is an AI assistant, not a lawyer. It can summarize and explain, but it cannot give you legal advice, predict how a court would rule, or know which laws apply in your specific situation. For anything with real consequences — signing a lease, accepting a job offer, disputing a charge — run the summary past a human professional.

## Step 1 — Get the text out of the document
Open the contract as a PDF or webpage and **copy the text** the way you would from any other file: click at the start, hold **Shift** and click at the end, then press **Ctrl+C** (Windows/Linux) or **Cmd+C** (macOS). On a phone, long-press in the text and choose **Select All**, then **Copy**. The text is now stored on your clipboard, ready to paste anywhere.
You'll know it worked when your clipboard holds a wall of text you can paste into a notes app or chat box to test.
**If it looks different:** some PDFs lock their text behind scanned images. If **Select All** only grabs a few words, try opening the PDF in Adobe Acrobat Reader, Google Drive, or your browser — they sometimes unlock the text layer. If that fails, use a free "PDF to text" tool online, or simply type the section headings you can see into Claude and ask it to explain what those usually mean. Don't paste a screenshot: Claude works with text, not images.

## Step 2 — Open Claude and start a fresh chat
Go to `claude.ai` in your browser, sign in, and click **New chat** in the sidebar (top-left). A blank conversation box appears at the bottom of the screen — that's where your message will go.
You'll know it worked when you see an empty message box with a **Send** arrow and a small **+** or paperclip-shaped attach icon nearby.
**If it looks different:** some accounts land directly in a recent conversation. Just look for a **+ New chat** or **Start new conversation** button at the top of the left sidebar. On the mobile app, look for a **+** or pencil icon in a corner to start fresh.

## Step 3 — Paste the contract and ask your first question
Click inside the message box and press **Ctrl+V** (Windows/Linux) or **Cmd+V** (macOS) to paste the long block of contract text *into the same message* as your question. Then add a clear request on a new line and hit **Send**.
💬 Example: "Here's the rental agreement I was sent. In plain language, what am I actually agreeing to? Highlight anything unusual or that renters often overlook."
You'll know it worked when Claude replies with a structured summary — usually with headings like *Key terms*, *Your obligations*, *What to watch out for* — instead of just echoing the text back at you.
**If it looks different:** if Claude's reply is short or feels generic, it may have ignored your question. Just send a second message asking for a clearer summary. If the contract is *very* long, you might see a "this is too long in one go" notice — move to **Step 4** for that workaround. Paid plans allow you to attach the PDF directly using a paperclip-style button next to the message box, which can skip the copy-paste step for shorter documents.

## Step 4 — Break the document into chunks if you got the "too long" notice
Claude can read a lot at once, but huge contracts can overflow the limit. **Open a notes app** and split the contract text into rough sections by hand: "Section 1 — Parties," "Section 2 — Term and Rent," "Section 3 — Deposits," and so on. Then send each chunk in its own message, with one short question per chunk.
💬 Example: "[Paste section 1 here] In one paragraph, summarize what this section says and flag anything I should negotiate."
You'll know it worked when each section gets its own focused answer with a small "what to watch out for" line. At the end, ask: "Based on everything I've pasted, give me a 5-bullet summary of the whole contract and the three most important things to push back on."
**If it looks different:** if you don't want to split the file manually, paid plans offer a much bigger context window — think of this as Claude's short-term memory: how much text it can keep in mind during one chat — and often fit a long contract without splitting. You can also try attaching the PDF directly with the paperclip button mentioned in Step 3, which is another way to handle longer documents.

## Step 5 — Ask targeted follow-up questions
Now that Claude has the document in its **context** (the chat's working memory: everything you've sent and received so far in this conversation), you can ask it pointed questions without re-pasting anything. This is where the real time-saving happens — most contracts only have four or five questions that actually matter to you.
💬 Example: "Can I get my security deposit back if I move out 30 days early?" or "If they change the price mid-contract, am I locked in?" or "What's the worst part of this agreement for me as the renter?"
You'll know it worked when Claude pulls a specific clause out of the text — usually with the section or clause number — and translates it into everyday language.
**If it looks different:** if Claude's answer feels vague, ask it to "quote the actual sentence from the contract" first, then re-explain it. That trick forces it to ground its answer in the real text instead of guessing.

## Step 6 — Save the summary somewhere you'll find it
Once you have a summary you trust, click the small **copy** icon at the corner of Claude's reply, or highlight the text and copy it the usual way. Paste it into an email to yourself, a note in your phone, or a shared doc with anyone who also needs to know.
💬 Example: "Save these notes and remind me to ask the landlord about the early-termination fee before I sign."
You'll know it worked when you have a plain-English record of the contract's main points, separate from the original legal document, that you can re-read in under five minutes.
**If it looks different:** Claude's chat history stays in your sidebar by default and you can reopen it from any device you're signed into. If you want a downloadable file, ask Claude: "Turn this summary into a Markdown checklist I can save" — it'll output one in chat that you can copy into a notes file.

## Common mistakes
- **Pasting a photo or screenshot of the contract.** Claude reads text, not images, unless you attach the file directly with the paperclip button in Step 3. Type or copy the actual text first whenever you can.
- **Asking one giant question like "explain this contract."** You'll get a wishy-washy answer. Ask for specific things: the cancellation terms, the fees, who's responsible for repairs, the auto-renewal clause.
- **Trusting the summary without checking.** Claude sometimes misreads a number or a date. If something matters to you, ask Claude to quote the original sentence so you can compare. For anything serious — money, a job, a home — confirm with a real lawyer or a free legal-aid clinic.
- **Sharing private contracts in public chats or forums.** Treat contract text like you would any sensitive document: only paste it into a private Claude chat tied to your own account.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** Before you click "I agree" on a new app's terms of service, the cleaning service's policy, or your kid's summer-camp registration, drop the text into Claude and ask "what's the catch?" You'll catch auto-renewal clauses and data-sharing sections that most people miss.
- **For your business or work:** When a client or vendor emails a 20-page service agreement, you can have a plain-English brief ready in minutes instead of bookmarking it for "later." Bring the brief — and your annotated questions — to whoever signs things for your business.
- **If you're just getting started:** Don't wait for a "big" contract to try this. A short terms-of-service page works fine to learn how to ask the right questions.

## Try it now
Pick one document in your email right now — even a four-paragraph cancellation policy from a gym or a streaming service you forgot to cancel. Paste it into a new Claude chat and ask: *"In plain language, what does this actually let them do? What's the catch?"* You'll have your answer in under a minute, and you'll know exactly how to repeat this the next time something bigger shows up.
